cues.txt: Welcome back to Job Search Stories by
Indeed. This week we're here to talk
about the uncomfortable truth that
maybe, just maybe, the traditional ways
of networking are broken. And maybe
there's a better way.
>> I'm Jen, a career coach and your go-to
gal for all things career advice.
>> And I'm Priya. We've got your back as
you take on the wild ride of job
hunting.
>> Welcome to Job Search Stories.
>> We dove back into Reddit and found a
story from someone about networking that
feels all too familiar. The title of
this post is not even networking is
working anymore, rant.
>> Has anyone else been struggling with
this? I've been working so hard to
network and get to know people in the
industry I want to be in. A lot of times
I will make a connection, I'll follow
up, they say they'll get back to me or
pass my info along, then I never hear
back. Having spent most of my job search
hearing it's all about who you know and
trying everything in my power to follow
that advice, it's getting so frustrating
having not even that work. What's hard
about this is that
>> the core advice itself isn't wrong.
Networking, it really does matter. But
the version we've been sold is totally
oversimplified. It leaves out the
timeline, the relationship building, and
most importantly, the long game. So, the
frustration here isn't a personal
failure, it's a gap between expectation
and reality. And I personally think
that's worth naming. What are some of
the networking tactics people have been
told to use that actually don't work the
way they used to?
>> The very first one that comes to mind is
just mass messaging.
>> Whole mass connection requests. Reaching
out to a high volume of people with the
same generic message. In a high volume
AI-driven world, this can really start
to feel like noise to somebody that's on
the receiving end. And it's not that the
reaching out is wrong, but when it's not
personalized, it's harder to stand out
or build a real connection. Another one
that I think is a little bit
oversimplified, or at least in the way
that we've thought about it, are
networking events. Attending events just
to collect contacts. Because in these
situations, you aren't actually building
a network, you're just collecting emails
or business cards. And in those
situations, most of the people that you
meet there may not even remember you,
and you definitely may not remember
them. Cuz the simple exchange of
information doesn't mean that you're
building a meaningful relationship. What
tends to matter more is whether or not
there's a moment of real connection or
even follow up after the event to keep
the connection warm.
>> someone at a networking event the other
day, and I very specifically told them
what I was going to follow up with them
about. I like the way you've built this
with your brand. I'd love to hear more
about someone doing that when they're
new to this. So, just being specific to,
I think, when you see them and following
up accordingly helps them remember you.
>> Absolutely. The last example that I can
think of is what we call the blast from
the past outreach. It's reaching to
somebody that you haven't spoken to in
months or years. There really is value
in reaching out to old contacts, but
those cold emails with no, "How have you
been?" can really feel and really are
transactional and cold. And it's just
important to remember that relationships
need to be nurtured. You want to keep a
connection warm and maintain contact
over time, even if it's sporadic. I
actually was just talking to someone the
other day who got that type of outreach.
And it was for an open role, but she
hadn't talked to this person in months.
And so, the connection really was, "Hey,
I saw this posting at your company. Can
you refer me to it?" And it's like, "Oh
my gosh, well, ask me how I've been. You
know, ask me how it's been since I to
this company." Just like a little bit of
warmth can just make the connection feel
a little bit stronger, and it doesn't
feel so out of the blue.
>> There's so much noise out there, and
people are getting so many messages,
whether it be their emails or on
networking sites. And so, it's really
important for you to stand out above the
noise and or make it personal. Like you
said, if you know that person, ask them
how they're doing, how they've been,
what their experience has been. So, I
think those are really important points,
Jen. Thank you for sharing that. A
recent national survey by the Harris
Poll confirms what many people are
feeling. They found that 79% of hiring
managers and 75% of job seekers say
networking today feels more like a
business transaction than a genuine
personal connection. As a career coach,
what makes you feel compelled to respond
or ignore a message when someone reaches
out to pick your brain?
>> Some things that make me respond is one,
if there's a relevant open role. If
you're reaching out about a position on
my team, I'm pretty much always happy to
talk. If it's elsewhere in the
organization, I'll usually try to point
you to the right person instead because
I'd rather redirect you to someone that
could actually give you useful
information than waste your time. I'll
also respond if there's a real
connection. If you mention that we
worked at the same company, we went to
the same school, or we even have a
mutual colleague or friend, then I'm
usually into the conversation. That
shared context actually means something
and it can signal that you really did
your homework before you even reached
out to me. I will say I will absolutely
give bonus points and more weight if
somebody in my network reaches out to me
directly about you and then you email me
directly versus reaching out on a
platform because the reality is I get
too many connection requests and it's
very difficult to sift through
sometimes. So, if I'm getting a request
and there's no message or no context,
I'll usually just ignore it because I
just can't read them all.
>> Even if you don't know me through a
connection, I think it's important to
put some effort into understanding who I
am and how we may be able to connect
successfully.
>> Yeah, cuz I'm always wondering like, why
me? Like, why are you reaching out to
me? And I'll also say like the last
thing that I will usually respond to is
if somebody connects with me and they're
asking about something that I genuinely
want to talk about. So, if the question
that you're asking is landing in my
wheelhouse or if it's on a topic that I
genuinely find interesting, then I'll
definitely make time. And so, if you're
trying to understand, well, how would I
know what somebody finds interesting?
Look at their history. Look what they're
posting about. Look what they're writing
articles about. Look at the types of
teams they're serving on. That's how you
get that information.
>> When I'm asking for things from other
people, similar to what you just said, I
try to put myself in their place in
terms of everything else they have going
on and make it a valuable use of their
time as well.
>> Priya, do you feel like applicants are
starting to appeal more to algorithmic
requirements instead of leading with
their authentic selves? And if so, does
this remove emotional connection from
networking?
>> Forbes reported that 2/3 of job seekers
are uncomfortable with AI evaluating
them, yet many feel they have no choice
but to adapt to it. The people who cut
through the noise, they lead with
something specific and real. I think
it's the exact same advice that we give
to job seekers when it comes to their
resume. Yes, run it through a tool, but
no one's going to have your specific
examples, your specific successes, and I
think that's what you need to think
about when you're reaching out to
people. I also think, and you mentioned
this several times, Jen, that having a
unique perspective, a story about why
you want to get to know them, a genuine
reason why you're reaching out, those
are the things that resonate with
people, not some perfectly polished
pitch. And I also believe that this is
why it's also important to approach
networking from a personal perspective
versus just through business
organizations. I think you and I have
talked several times about how community
organizations, sporting organizations,
anything else that you're involved in
can also be a way to network as well.
And I think people should really expand
their scope when it comes to that.
Priya, when was the last time you
referred someone to a role from a
non-traditional networking interaction?
>> I referred a woman who was returning to
the workforce after I'd worked with her
on our school parents association board.
And so, I'd worked with her just in a
partner capacity, and she was so
organized, had great ideas, very
creative and critical thinker. And so,
when a role came across my radar, she
was the first person I thought of. Not
because she'd ever ask me to keep her in
mind, but because I already knew her,
and that familiarity did all the work.
So, that's why I always talk about
non-traditional networking. It works
precisely because there's no agenda.
You're just a person being a person and
working with someone in a different
capacity, and the professional
connection follows naturally. And the
great news was it was a great fit for
her. She did end up taking the job, and
she's extremely happy. Not every story
is a Cinderella story, but this one
worked out really well, and I think,
again, that's why working with people in
other capacities beyond your current job
or professional networking groups can
help open doors for you.
>> Within networking, when you're
connecting to an alumni group or shared
interest or kind of whatever that is,
you're connecting the dots for that
person to say like, "This is the
intention. This is the reason I'm
reaching out to you. It's not just
because I found you out there." You're
explaining the why.
>> Do you think networking can become
transactional instead of human?
>> In a market where so many people are
reaching out, networking can start to
feel transactional. Messages can come
across like sales pitches, even when
that's not the intention. And when that
happens, it becomes harder to build real
connections. So, a transactional message
would sound something like, "Hi, I'm
currently looking for a job. Can you
refer me or connect me to someone on
your team?" You're just asking for
something. So, conversely, an example of
a more human approach would sound
something like, "Hi, I came across your
work on X, and I found your perspective
on Y really interesting. I'd love to
hear how you got into this space, if
you're open to sharing." Networking is
really about the long game. Yes, some
people do make cold outreaches and land
opportunities, but that really isn't the
case for everyone and those results are
not typical.
>> Jen, have you ever felt like you were
bothering someone when reaching out with
intention of networking?
>> I've never felt like I was bothering
somebody when I was reaching out with
the intention of networking. This is my
career. I inundate myself with like
learning strategies and so with that I
get very comfortable with them. But I
would say that I do get anxiety when I'm
reaching out to people I don't know. And
that really is a different thing and I
think it's really important that we
separate the two ideas because the fear
of bothering someone and the anxiety of
cold outreach are really not the same
feeling. One is about being a burden and
the other is about vulnerability,
putting yourself out there with no
guarantee of getting a response. And
it's really easy to complete the two,
but if you understand which one you're
feeling, you can really change the way
that you handle it. So in my opinion,
you should feel comfortable reaching out
to network when you have something
specific to say or to ask. Big requests
can feel burdensome, that's for sure.
But a focused, respectful ask is easy to
respond to or to decline graciously. The
specificity is what separates a good
outreach from an awkward one.
>> Along those lines, would you say that
most networking wins are invisible at
first?
>> Yeah, I would absolutely say that. There
was a comment on Reddit that I feel sums
up the benefits of networking really
well. Yes, networking still works, but
the expectation is wrong when you expect
it to immediately bring you a job lead.
You could meet someone and then later on
it could lead to a role, but networking
is not a job search strategy that
commonly gives instant results. It's
really like planting seeds. Nothing
looks different the next day, but
underground something may already be
growing.
>> You mentioned Jen, it's a long game. I
personally can be impatient sometimes
and I know that many of our job seekers
are as well. So, what are signs that
networking is working even if the
results aren't visible yet? The mistake
many people make is measuring it by
outcomes like a job offer or an
introduction or an opportunity. But
those are some of the last things that
happen. They're not typically the first.
So, the signals that you should be
looking for are things like when people
remember your name without prompting.
You stop having to reintroduce yourself
or, you know, somebody mentions you in a
room that you weren't even in. Another
signal would be when responses are
getting warmer over time. You went from
a one-word reply to a paragraph, from a
thanks to connecting to let me know if
you ever want to chat. You can really
tell how the relationship is growing
just by the temperature of the response.
Another signal is you're having repeat
conversations. One exchange is a
contact. Opening dialogue is a
relationship. So, if somebody is coming
back to talk, you're really building
something real. Another last sign would
be if you become somebody's go-to for
something. People start tagging you,
they start forwarding you an article or
saying, "Oh, you should really reach out
to so-and-so for that." Being associated
with a topic or expertise
is a major signal. So, while the results
might be invisible, that doesn't mean
that the work itself is invisible. Just
remember that timelines for networking
success, if you will, can really vary by
your industry, seniority, and your
goals. So, if things are feeling slow
for you, that doesn't necessarily mean
that progress is stalled. You have to be
open about the fact that you're willing
to give your time back to them as well.
And often when I send networking
messages to people I know well, I always
end it with, "Please let me know if I
can ever help you with anything or be a
resource to you for anything." And I
think even putting that out there in
email shows them that you want this to
be a two-way relationship. The real
magic of effective networking comes down
to one word, familiarity. Reaching out
once may still leave you in the stranger
category. What you're actually working
toward is the moment when a recruiter,
hiring manager, or contact thinks, "I've
seen your name before. We've talked to
you times. I feel like I know you.
>> Networking doesn't work in a straight
line. It works in the background. Your
efforts are definitely non-linear. With
job applications, you at least get a
confirmation that your application was
received, at least most of the time.
With networking, you might send a
thoughtful message, have a great
conversation, and then nothing happens
for months or even years. I've seen it
play out enough times to believe that
those seeds do grow. What I really want
job seekers to keep in mind is that the
work is real even when those results are
invisible yet. I know it's a hard thing
to hold on to when you're actively job
searching and you need something to
happen right now.
>> That's the thing about networking is we
think about how effective a strategy it
can be. It's often not most effective in
the here and now. It's most effective
when you've built the relationship and
then you're going to have a positive
outcome from it.
>> So, if you've been putting in the effort
and not seeing results yet, that doesn't
mean nothing is happening. It might just
mean it hasn't shown up yet. And next
week, we're breaking down what actually
works, [music]
the tactics that move the needle, and
how to approach networking in a way that
feels a lot more human. Stay tuned for
part two of our deep dive into
networking. And if any of this resonates
with you, be sure to like, follow, and
subscribe for more job search stories
[music] that just may help remind you
that you're not alone out there.
